svg.title: A journey with room to spare

text.tspan: Everyday English - C1 - 2026/10/18 - Essay - 01
Travelers look at a map to consider their route.
Pexels · 12585781
A journey with room to spare
The decision to plan a short trip may appear ordinary, yet it exposes a recurring tension between arrangements that make life manageable
and experiences that resist being prescribed. A defensible approach combines proportionate preparation with a willingness to reconsider
whose interests a plan serves.
Preparation has value because checking the route reduces avoidable confusion. In the present case, we write down the platform and the time
of the last train. Such an intervention is modest, but that modesty is its strength: it removes a foreseeable obstacle without claiming to
determine the entire experience. Structure is useful to the extent that it releases attention rather than consuming it.
That argument requires a qualification, however: leaving spare time makes changes easier to manage. For instance, we choose an earlier bus
rather than risk missing our connection. An arrangement that appears efficient from one standpoint may impose costs elsewhere. Listening to
those affected is therefore not an optional gesture of goodwill; it supplies information without which the plan cannot be adequately evaluated.
The resulting principle is one of proportion. Preparation deserves support when it clarifies responsibilities and protects time, while
responsiveness prevents it from hardening into an end in itself. To judge the experience well is to examine both what the arrangement
enables and what it may inadvertently exclude.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body
paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Persuade a group to change how they plan a short trip. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a practical example of
each. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion.
